planting.note: Plant container-grown stock in spring in moist, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; this male selection establishes and grows noticeably faster than seedling-grown fringetrees.

directions: 'Dirr' is a male clone of white fringetree selected in Georgia for its markedly faster growth rate in the nursery row compared to typical seedling stock, reaching landscape size in less time without sacrificing the species' signature floral display. In late spring it produces the airy, drooping panicles of strap-shaped white petals characteristic of the species, and because it is a male selection the flower clusters tend to be fuller and more fragrant, though no fruit is set. Its leaves are noticeably larger and a deeper glossy green than many other named fringetree clones, giving it a bolder summer presence in the landscape. Grow it as a specimen or understory tree in full sun to light shade with consistent moisture, and expect the same long-lived, low-maintenance performance that makes the species a garden favorite.
sources: Trees and Shrubs Online (International Dendrology Society) — Chionanthus virginicus
Dirr, M.A. — Manual of Woody Landscape Plants

planting.note: Plant container-grown stock in spring in moist, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; this older male selection forms a dense, upright crown.

directions: 'Floyd' is one of the older named selections of white fringetree, originating as a seedling in an Illinois experimental garden in the 1940s and later propagated and distributed as a distinct clone. As a male selection, it produces unusually dense, heavy clusters of the species' fragrant white, ribbon-petaled flowers each spring without the later litter of fruit, and its habit is more upright and tidy than the sprawling multi-stemmed form typical of wild seedlings. The tighter, more tree-like crown makes it easier to site as a specimen near patios or walkways where a looser-growing fringetree might feel unruly. Give it full sun to partial shade and even moisture while young; once established it is tough, adaptable, and essentially trouble-free.
sources: Trees and Shrubs Online (International Dendrology Society) — Chionanthus virginicus
Dirr, M.A. — Manual of Woody Landscape Plants

planting.note: Plant container-grown stock in spring in moist, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; this Maryland-origin selection flowers heavily even on young plants.

directions: 'White Knight' was selected at a Maryland nursery for its precocious flowering, covering itself in the species' trademark drooping white fringe-like blooms within just a few years of planting rather than the decade or more some seedling fringetrees take to reach full flowering maturity. Its leaves are shiny and leathery compared to the softer, matte foliage of wild-type plants, giving the tree a more polished, refined look through the growing season. Like other named fringetree clones it is propagated by grafting or cutting to preserve this precocious, heavy-flowering trait rather than left to chance seedling variation. Site it in full sun to partial shade with consistently moist, well-drained soil for the best floral display.
sources: Trees and Shrubs Online (International Dendrology Society) — Chionanthus virginicus

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in early spring in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade; variegated foliage colors best with some protection from hot midday sun.

directions: 'Silver Splash' arose as a chance branch mutation on a Carolina silverbell growing at a Pennsylvania arboretum and was propagated for its boldly variegated foliage, with irregular creamy-white splashes scattered across otherwise dark green leaves. Like the species it bears pendant clusters of white, bell-shaped flowers along bare branches in April and May before the leaves fully emerge, but once the foliage expands the variegation becomes the season-long ornamental feature, brightening shaded woodland plantings long after the bloom has passed. It shares the species' preference for moist, humus-rich, acidic soil and dappled shade beneath taller canopy trees, and grows with the same airy, horizontally branched habit. Because the variegation is a sport rather than a seed-grown trait, propagate by cutting or grafting to keep the pattern stable, and watch for and remove any plain-green reversion shoots.
sources: Broken Arrow Nursery plant catalog — Halesia tetraptera 'Silver Splash'
Dirr, M.A. — Manual of Woody Landscape Plants

planting.note: Plant container-grown stock in spring in moist, acidic, well-drained soil; give it some afternoon shade, since the cream-white leaf margins can scorch in hot, intense sun.

directions: 'Frosted Emerald' is a variegated Japanese snowbell selection from an Oregon nursery, grown for its irregularly patterned foliage rather than flower color alone — leaves show cream-white margins in sunnier spots or can become almost entirely cream-white with scattered green blotches when grown in shadier conditions. It still produces the species' pendant white, bell-shaped spring flowers beneath its horizontal branches, but its slower growth rate and smaller mature size compared to the plain green species make it a better fit for smaller gardens or as a container specimen. The variegated foliage is prone to occasional green reversion shoots, which should be pruned out to keep the plant's patterned look, and leaves can scorch if exposed to strong, direct afternoon sun. Site it in part shade with shelter from harsh wind and consistent soil moisture for the best color development.
sources: Plantlust nursery plant database — Styrax japonicus 'Frosted Emerald'

planting.note: Plant container-grown stock in spring in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; its weeping habit benefits from a short trunk standard to show off the cascading branches.

directions: 'Nightfall' is a patented J. Frank Schmidt & Son introduction that combines two traits previously found only in separate Japanese snowbell cultivars — the deep purple-black foliage of purple-leaved selections and the gracefully weeping branch habit of cascading green-leaved forms. Creamy white, bell-shaped flowers with pearly buds open against the dark foliage backdrop in late spring, giving strong color contrast that larger upright purple selections cannot match. Its compact, cascading form fits easily into small gardens or near patios where a full-size snowbell would be too large, and the dense weeping branches give it an attractive sculptural silhouette even in winter. Grow it in moist, acidic, well-drained soil with some afternoon shade in hot climates to keep the foliage color from fading.
sources: J. Frank Schmidt & Son Co. nursery introductions catalog
Oregon Association of Nurseries New Varieties Showcase records

planting.note: Plant container-grown stock in spring in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; its delayed bud break makes it a good choice for sites prone to late spring frosts.

directions: 'Spring Showers' was released by the U.S. National Arboretum's breeding program from an open-pollinated seedling population, selected specifically because its leaves and flower buds emerge two to three weeks later than typical Japanese snowbell seedlings, letting it dodge the late-season freezes that can damage early-breaking trees. It grows into a small, tightly conical tree rather than the broader vase shape of the species, making it a good fit for narrower planting strips. Fragrant white, bell-shaped flowers about three-quarters of an inch across hang beneath the foliage in late spring, slightly later than most other snowbell selections. Plant it in moist, acidic, well-drained soil with some afternoon shade in hotter climates for best performance.
sources: U.S. National Arboretum new plant release notes — Styrax japonicus 'Spring Showers'
J. Frank Schmidt & Son Co. nursery introductions catalog
